label: Comparison Theory
notes: This chapter, printed pages 319 to 344, asks how curvature bounds translate into hard geometric and topological conclusions. We meet the Riccati equation, Jacobi field comparison, Rauch, Bonnet-Myers, Cartan-Hadamard, and Bishop-Gromov, all flowing from one principle: bound curvature, control geodesic spreading.

label: Constant-Curvature Models
notes: Everything is measured against three reference spaces of constant curvature. The sphere closes geodesics and refocuses them, Euclidean space spreads them linearly, and hyperbolic space spreads them exponentially. The functions sin, identity, and sinh are the universal yardsticks the comparison theorems use.

label: Jacobi Fields
notes: A Jacobi field measures the first-order separation between a geodesic and its infinitesimal neighbors. It solves a linear second-order equation driven by the curvature operator. Where a nontrivial Jacobi field vanishes at both ends we find conjugate points, the precise failure of geodesics to minimize.

label: The Riccati Equation
notes: Differentiating the shape operator of distance spheres converts the second-order Jacobi equation into a first-order matrix Riccati equation. The Riccati form is monotone in curvature, which is exactly why curvature inequalities propagate to inequalities on the Hessian of the distance function and on volume growth.

label: Hessian of Distance
notes: The Hessian of the distance function is the shape operator of geodesic spheres and obeys the Riccati equation. Comparing it against the model value gives sharp upper or lower bounds on how distance spheres curve, the analytic engine behind both Laplacian and volume comparison results.

label: Rauch Comparison
notes: The Rauch comparison theorem says larger curvature shrinks Jacobi fields and smaller curvature stretches them. If sectional curvature stays below a bound, geodesics spread at least as fast as in the model, pushing conjugate points farther out and controlling the differential of the exponential map.

label: Conjugate Points
notes: A sectional curvature upper bound delays conjugate points; a positive lower bound forces them to appear by a fixed distance. Past a conjugate point a geodesic no longer minimizes. This dual control of focusing is the bridge from Rauch to the global Bonnet-Myers diameter estimate.

label: Bonnet-Myers Theorem
notes: If Ricci curvature is bounded below by a positive constant, every geodesic of length beyond pi over root of that bound carries a conjugate point, so it cannot minimize. The manifold therefore has finite diameter, is compact by Hopf-Rinow, and has finite fundamental group.

label: Cartan-Hadamard Theorem
notes: With nonpositive sectional curvature no conjugate points ever form, so the exponential map at any point is a covering map. A complete simply connected manifold of nonpositive curvature is therefore diffeomorphic to Euclidean space, and any two points are joined by a unique geodesic.

label: Bishop-Gromov Volume
notes: Integrating the Riccati Hessian bound under a Ricci lower bound shows that the ratio of the volume of a metric ball to the model ball of the same radius is nonincreasing in radius. This monotone ratio is the foundation of modern volume comparison and convergence theory.

label: Spreading Compared
notes: Side by side, Jacobi field magnitudes under an upper curvature bound stay above the model curve while those under a lower bound stay below it. The model functions sin, linear, and sinh frame every actual geodesic, making spreading and refocusing a quantitative, checkable statement.

label: Synthesis
notes: Comparison theory is one idea applied repeatedly: a curvature inequality enters the Riccati equation and exits as a bound on Jacobi fields, conjugate points, diameter, or volume. Bonnet-Myers, Cartan-Hadamard, and Bishop-Gromov are three faces of that single monotonicity principle.
